##### **Greek political machinations fuel market uncertainty and volatility** 

Markets saw a rebound after the sell-off at the beginning of LME Week, but were unable to hold onto their gains as Euro Zone sovereign debt problems regained their grip on sentiment.  At the fore has been the uncertainty caused by the Greek debt issue which was further exacerbated by the Prime Minister’s decision to put the imposed ba

ilout and austerity measures to a public referendum.  Having put markets into a tailspin, the subsequent decision to reverse this proposal (following intense pressure from both within and without the country), allowed equity and commodity markets to recover ground.  Nevertheless, the ensuing political upheaval within Greece has left the markets on edge.

In Japan, aluminium premiums have been pressured by the demand impact on the Thai operations of Japanese manufactures caused by the floods in the country.  Nickel markets are feeling the effects of further deterioration in stainless steel activity, especially in some European areas and in North America.  Meanwhile, the copper market is gaining some support from ongoing strike action at Grasberg and a decline in scrap availability.  Tin prices have also been relatively buoyed by collective action from Indonesian producers, whilst zinc premiums seem to be reflecting some positive effects from ongoing cash-and-carry trades locking in LME inventories. 

While concerns continue over Greece, they also remain in place for other vulnerable European economies (especially regarding the potential domino-effect of a Greek default), particularly those considered “too big to fail”, Italy and Spain.  Until the main Euro Zone issues are resolved, or at least a credible plan of action outlined, we expect to see a continuation of market volatility. Also, despite prices having already retreated from historical as well as recent highs, we still see further downside risk.  The GFMS’ base metal index is an average of all the base metals rather than the LMEX, which is heavily weighted towards the performance of aluminium and copper.   Following a 6.3% fall in September, the Index plunged a further 10.5% in October (on a monthly average basis). 

###### **Recent economic indicators display some regional differences** 

Europe exhibited general weakness: the German PMI fell to 48.9 in October, signalling the end of a 27-month period of continuous expansion, whilst the EU PMI contracted further, to 47.1; year-on-year German industrial production and retail sales came in considerably lower than expected for September, at 5.4% and 0.3%, respectively; German and EU unemployment also both edged higher than consensus estimates.  Against this backdrop, and that of the sovereign debt troubles, the ECB caught markets by surprise by implementing a 25 basis point cut in its benchmark rate. 

Apart from an unexpectedly low print of 9.1% for Q3 GDP, recent Chinese data have suggested that the economy is continuing to motor ahead.  September industrial production was recorded at 13.8%, year-on-year, and retail sales were up on the previous year by 17.7%.  The Chinese PMI, which had just fallen below 50 in September, registered 51.0 for October.

New orders rose from 49.6 to 52.4, its highest level since April. Conditions in the Euro zone have continued to deteriorate, with the Euro zone economic sentiment index falling, albeit slightly, in October to 94.8, the lowest level in almost two years, from 95 in the previous month. Concerns about the adverse impact of Europe’s sovereign debt crisis, and fiscal tightening throughout the Euro zone, on the economy weighed on the confidence of manufacturers, service providers and consumers. Overall, sentiment will remain under pressure in the coming months. Germany has also come under pressure in recent times, with industrial production dropping 2.4% month-on-month in September, following a 0.4% fall in August. While domestic demand is expected to ease on subdued household spending and weak economic growth, muted foreign demand will be the main drag on the German industry. As such, growth is expected to continue to disappoint till the first half of 2012, before it starts to pick up. Japanese industrial production slumped 4% in September from August, much sharper than expected. Car output dropped sharply following gains in recent months. Production of electronic goods also tumbled, particularly semiconductors, on the back of weak global demand, competition from lower-cost producers elsewhere, and a strong yen. Aluminium - November 2011 











##### **Aluminium** 

###### **Recent developments** 

- **_Whilst aluminium prices have not exhibited the same degree of volatility as other metals on the LME complex, they have nevertheless traded within a 13-14% range during September and October. At the time of writing, cash aluminium was trading at around $2,100/tonne, almost 5% lower than its close at the end of September._** 

- **_The rate of decline in LME stocks slowed in October, with a net outflow of just 16,000 tonnes during the month.  Meanwhile, Shanghai Exchange inventories registered an increase of 113,000 tonnes in October.  Adding anecdotal reports of off-warrant stock build in Rotterdam, these numbers portray a more uncertain demand environment in the midst of ongoing turmoil in Euro Zone sovereign debt negotiations._** 

- **_Weaker sentiment has also been reflected in steady to lower physical premiums over the last month in all major regions.  Japanese traders have cited the impact of the floods negatively impacting Japanese auto and electrical appliance manufacturing in Thailand, as a cause for weakness in spot premiums. Aluminium companies have also been sounding some notes of caution about the demand environment, with both Sapa and Hydro doing so in Europe, joined by Chalco (which has referenced the potential impact of Chinese government tightening on its customers)._** 

###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** 

- **_The short term outlook continues to be dominated by the Greek (and wider European) debt crisis, which met a further recent twist as the Greek government proposed, and then subsequently withdrew, plans for a public referendum on its bailout conditions and austerity measures.  Adding extra uncertainty has been the sudden collapse into bankruptcy of major commodity broker MF Global._** 

- **_Given the market uncertainty and volatility, we have not made any major revisions to our outlook over the next 12 months.  We await some clarity on the European situation as well as any potential policy response in the US. Macroeconomic and financial markets remain the main determinants for demand prospects and prices in the near term._** 

- **_However, we have slightly increased our market surpluses for 2011 and 2012, to 640,000 tonnes and 275,000 tonnes, respectively. Thomson Reuters GFMS is forecasting an annual average price of $2,500/ tonne in 2012._**

###### **Market background** At the time of writing, the cash aluminium price had fallen by more than 12% since the beginning of September (to $2,120/tonne), and it was trading almost 1% below the low close seen at the beginning of LME Week. Aluminium price movements were, however, the most sedate of those on the base metals complex; for example, the cash copper price moved by -14% and +16% over the same periods. The Euro Zone sovereign debt issues continue to overhang the market and are dominating near-term price movements. It is likely that this will continue for some time, especially if a credible solution is not tabled soon. Nevertheless, the aluminium price’s proximity to its global marginal cost of production is lending some underlying support, as are energy prices, which have remained relatively resilient. Brent crude oil, apart from a brief fall to below $100/bbl during the commodity sell-off at the start of October, has continued to trade well above that level in recent weeks. **...as caution reigns over fallout from European crisis** The limited inventory offtake last month may reflect growing uncertainty over the outcome of the Euro Zone crisis and its potential impact on demand. This also ties in with anecdotal reports of some pockets of softness in consumer interest. Whilst there have been signs of continued demand from Germany and northern Europe, especially from the auto sector, southern European demand has been understandably weaker. The extrusion sector, in particular, seems to be experiencing a slowdown, with some consumers reported to pr

efer to delay orders and purchase hand-to-mouth. ###### **September inventory reduction not repeated in October...** The reported stock decline seen in September did not follow through into October, at least as far as exchange stocks are concerned. LME stocks of primary aluminium fell by 1.5% (69,000 tonnes) in September, but by only 0.3% (16,000 tonnes) in October, to 4.548 million tonnes. Meanwhile, Shanghai exchange stocks, which had fallen from around 125,000 tonnes to 77,000 tonnes in September, had increased to over 113,000 tonnes by the end of October. There have also been anecdotal reports indicating that a significant tonnage of aluminium is sitting off-warrant in Rotterdam, and that much of this has built up in the last few months. This sentiment has been reinforced by some of the major European producers. Sapa has said that it is “seeing a trend of softening markets in the extrusion business in all regions in Europe as well as in North America”. Hydro, whilst maintaining its view that global aluminium demand will rise by 7% in 2011, said that “markets had weakened and that growth may come in on the low side”. (For comparison, Thomson Reuters GFMS sees 5.8% growth in consumption this year.) The Hydro CEO was also recently quoted as saying that “[their] customers are becoming more nervous and are reducing their inventories”. The latest producer stocks from the International Aluminium Institute (IAI), up to end-September, showed that unwrought inventories of primary aluminium fell by 4.8% over the month, to 1.414 million tonnes. In addition, reports indicate that aluminium stocks at major Japanese ports fell by almost 10,000 tonnes during September, to 231,400 tonnes. ###### **Global consumption firms in August...** 

According to the latest data from the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), global demand through August 2011 was 5.1% higher year-on-year.  Following a month-on-month fall in consumption in July of 4.5%, world demand recovered in August to post a monthly increase of 1.5%. 

European demand recovered in August, with WBMS data showing 0.7% growth compared with the previous month (July data showed a 6.6% fall, driven by double-digit monthon-month declines in Italy, Spain and France – amongst others – more than offsetting a 9% increase in Germany). In August, German and French demand was estimated to have fallen by 4.9% and 6.7%, respectively, limiting European growth as a whole. 

According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), automobile sales rose by 19.2% month-on-month in September to about 1.65 million units. For the whole nine months of the year, auto sales reached 13.63 million units, up by 3.6% year-on-year.  CAAM’s forecast for 2011 is for China’s auto sales to grow by 3-5% to over 18.6 million units. 

A note of caution was, however, sounded by Chalco, China’s largest aluminium producer, which missed its Q3 earnings forecast; the same month when Chinese GDP figures for Q3 were reported at a lower-than-expected 9.1%.  The company expressed concern about potential payment defaults from its domestic customers due to scarcer credit, in an environment where reserve ratios and interest rates have been rising. 

Japanese consumption recovered sharply in August, according to the WBMS, whilst US demand followed a 7% decline in July with a further 15.8% fall in August. 

###### **Aluminium supply growth keeping pace with demand** 

IAI production estimates show that the daily rate of global production of primary aluminium continued to edge higher. For the year through September, cumulative production registered a 6.6% increase on the same period last year.  On an annualised basis, the IAI data point to total production of 43.8 million tonnes, with increased output in China and the Middle East being the main drivers. 

###### **...with China continuing to be a major driver** 

Chinese demand was estimated by the WBMS to be 2.3% higher, month-on-month in August, meaning that over January-August as a whole, consumption grew by 6.2% year-on-year. Given the lack of new projects in the pipeline, any supply response would be limited in scope, intensifying the market tightness and leading prices to annual averages of $26,850/ tonne and $27,625/tonne over 2011 and 2012 respectively. 

Given the acute market tightness, the downside for tin under our **low case scenario C** is less severe than that for the other base metals.  Whilst demand side underperformance would therefore see prices slide from current levels, we expect average prices to remain comparatively well supported at $25,850/tonne and $18,000/tonne over 2011 and 2012 respectively.
